name: Linked List Patterns
tagline: Trading O(1) random indexing and CPU cache locality for O(1) pointer-based splicing, reversal, and LRU eviction.
purpose: Master sentinel dummy heads, fast/slow pointers, and HashMap + Doubly-Linked-List hybrids used in LRU caches, OS kernel lists, and Redis Skip Lists.

spark.summary: Linked lists trade O(1) random indexing and CPU cache locality for O(1) pointer-based splicing, reversal, and eviction without shifting contiguous memory.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use sentinel dummy heads, fast/slow pointers, and HashMap+Doubly-Linked-List hybrids (LRU) to eliminate edge-case bugs and achieve O(1) structural mutations.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** A **linked list** stores elements in heap-allocated nodes connected by pointers (`next`, and `prev` for doubly linked lists) rather than contiguous memory.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts HashMap Index + Doubly Linked List Recency Chain (HashMap<K, Node> -> Dummy Head <-> MRU -> LRU <-> Dummy Tail -> Node(key, val)); 3-Pointer Reversal Invariant (Capture Next Before Mutating) (1. SAVE NEXT -> 2. FLIP LINK -> 3. ADVANCE).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Pointer count, concurrency friendliness, and cache behavior determine the right linear structure. In systems programming (Linux `struct list_head`), embedding link pointers *inside* the payload struct avoids double heap allocations.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Apply linked list splicing and O(1) eviction patterns to classic LLD and systems problems.

learningJourney.title: What are Linked List Patterns
learningJourney.explanation:
A **linked list** stores elements in heap-allocated nodes connected by pointers (`next`, and `prev` for doubly linked lists) rather than contiguous memory.

Three foundational patterns eliminate most pointer bugs and unlock $O(1)$ structural updates:
- **Sentinel Dummy Head/Tail**: eliminates `if (head == null)` special cases during head insertion/deletion.
- **Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd's Tortoise & Hare)**: finds midpoints and detects cycles in $O(N)$ time, $O(1)$ space.
- **HashMap + Doubly Linked List**: powers $O(1)$ get/put/evict in LRU caches.

sectionDiagram.title: HashMap Index + Doubly Linked List Recency Chain

cards.label: 1. O(1) Lookup
cards.detail: HashMap jumps directly to the heap node without traversing the list.

cards.label: 2. O(1) Promotion
cards.detail: Unlink node via prev/next and insert right after Dummy Head.

cards.label: 3. O(1) Eviction
cards.detail: When full, unlink tail.prev and delete its key from the HashMap.

sectionDiagram.summary: Combining a HashMap with sentinel-bounded doubly linked nodes turns O(N) list search into O(1) end-to-end LRU operations.

learningJourney.title: Why pointer splicing still matters despite CPU cache locality
learningJourney.explanation:
Contiguous arrays (`std::vector`, `ArrayList`) win 95% of general workloads because sequential elements fit in 64-byte CPU cache lines. However, arrays require $O(N)$ element shifting on middle removal and periodic $O(N)$ reallocation pauses.

Wherever you already hold a node reference and need **$O(1)$ middle removal/promotion without reallocation**—such as OS kernel intrusive lists (`struct list_head`), timer wheels, or LRU/LFU eviction queues—linked-list patterns are indispensable.

sectionDiagram.title: 3-Pointer Reversal Invariant (Capture Next Before Mutating)
sectionDiagram.summary: Always capture nxt = curr.next before overwriting curr.next = prev; otherwise the rest of the list is lost.

learningJourney.explanation: Pointer count, concurrency friendliness, and cache behavior determine the right linear structure.

benefits: O(1) arbitrary removal given a node pointer; zero O(N) resize pauses.
costs: 2x pointer overhead and poor spatial locality.

benefits: Half the pointer overhead; ideal for lock-free CAS stacks (Treiber stack).
costs: Deleting an arbitrary node requires O(N) traversal to find its predecessor.

benefits: No tree rotations; simpler fine-grained locking and range scans.
costs: Probabilistic O(log N) rather than strict deterministic height.

learningJourney.title: Intrusive Lists & Lock-Free ABA Mitigation
learningJourney.explanation: In systems programming (Linux `struct list_head`), embedding link pointers *inside* the payload struct avoids double heap allocations. In lock-free CAS linked lists, **tagged pointers** (64-bit pointer + 64-bit monotonic version) or epoch-based reclamation prevent the **ABA problem** where a freed-and-reused node tricks `CAS` into corrupting the list.

ideas.title: Intrusive List Advantage
ideas.description: One allocation per object instead of separate node wrapper + payload allocations, cutting allocator fragmentation.

ideas.title: ABA Prevention
ideas.description: Pair pointer CAS with a monotonic version counter (`cmpxchg16b`) or hazard pointers before reclaiming unlinked nodes.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does a production LRU Cache pair a HashMap with a Doubly Linked List instead of a Singly Linked List?

options.text: Singly linked lists cannot store key-value pairs
options.feedback: Any node can store key-value fields; the limitation is unlinking.

options.text: Unlinking an arbitrary middle node in O(1) requires direct access to its predecessor (prev), which a singly linked list lacks
options.feedback: Correct: on a cache hit, the HashMap gives the node pointer, and prev/next pointers unlink and promote it to MRU in O(1).

options.text: Doubly linked lists use half as much memory per node
options.feedback: Doubly linked lists use twice as many pointers (prev and next).
